plants.name: Camellia japonica
plants.description: Glossy evergreen shrubs and small trees break the winter gloom with rose-like blooms in crimson, blush pink and white. Each flower sits close along the branch and glows against dark, polished leaves. In coastal woodlands it is a welcome splash of colour when little else is flowering.
plants.bloomingSeason: Wild plants flower from about January to March, so late January falls within the season.
plants.location: Coastal woodlands and gardens of Japan, South Korea and nearby East Asia
plants.funFact: Camellia japonica is a close cousin of the tea plant, Camellia sinensis. Both belong to the same genus.

plants.name: Prunus mume
plants.description: Ume are among the first trees to blossom each year, with fragrant, rounded-petal flowers that open on bare branches, sometimes against a dusting of snow. Their sweet, spicy perfume drifts through shrines, parks and orchards.
plants.bloomingSeason: January to February in Japan, so late January sits in the early part of the season.
plants.location: Gardens, shrines and orchards across Japan, especially in milder regions
plants.funFact: Ume bloom weeks before cherry blossoms. You can tell them apart by their rounded petals, while sakura petals have a notched tip.

plants.name: Protea cynaroides
plants.description: South Africa's national flower is a showy, dinner-plate-sized bloom. Its crown of pink-tipped bracts surrounds a silky centre, and it flowers in the heat of the southern summer on tough, leathery-leaved shrubs.
plants.bloomingSeason: Some populations flower in summer, from January to March, in the Western Cape.
plants.location: Fynbos of South Africa's Western Cape, including coastal areas such as Phillipskop
plants.funFact: The King Protea has the largest flower head in the protea family. At some sites a typical red form flowers in summer, and a white form flowers in winter.
